title: Introduction to Minimum Spanning Tree (Prim)
description: Grow a minimum spanning tree from one node, always adding the cheapest frontier edge

blocks.text: Prim algorithm is the second classic way to build a minimum spanning tree, the cheapest set of edges that connects every node of a weighted graph. Where Kruskal sorts all edges globally, Prim grows a single tree outward from a starting node.
At each step it looks at every edge leaving the tree built so far and adds the cheapest one that reaches a new node. A priority queue makes finding that cheapest edge fast.

blocks.caption: Prim grows one tree outward from a start node, adding the cheapest reaching edge
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761241-641019302.png

By the end of this topic you will understand how Prim grows its tree, why a priority queue is the right tool, the full algorithm and code, why the greedy choice is optimal, its complexity, and when to prefer it over Kruskal. It is a must know graph algorithm.
If Kruskal is the algorithm that thinks about edges, Prim is the one that thinks about nodes. Both reach the same minimum spanning tree by different routes.
Keep the single growing tree image in mind, because it is what separates Prim from Kruskal at every step.
Prim builds a minimum spanning tree incrementally, starting from any single node and expanding one node at a time until the tree spans the whole graph.
The tree is always a single connected piece throughout the process. Prim never has separate fragments; it grows one blob outward, absorbing the nearest new node at every step.

items: Starts from a single arbitrary node
Grows one connected tree, never a forest
Adds the cheapest edge reaching a node not yet included
Finishes when every node is in the tree

blocks.text:
One growing tree:

The defining image of Prim is a single tree that keeps swallowing its nearest neighbour. Contrast that with Kruskal, which merges many small fragments.
Because the tree is always connected, at any moment you already have a valid tree over the nodes you have absorbed, just not yet a spanning one.

items: Pick any node to seed the tree
Repeatedly absorb the nearest outside node
Never maintain separate fragments
End with a single tree covering all nodes

blocks.text: This incremental growth is what makes Prim feel like a flood spreading out from a source, always claiming the nearest new ground.
Think of the nodes as split into two sets: those already in the tree, and those still outside it. Prim repeatedly moves one node from outside to inside.

blocks.caption: The tree starts as one node and grows outward, absorbing one node per step
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761242-328720832.png
To decide which outside node to absorb next, Prim looks at the boundary between the two sets, and picks the cheapest edge that crosses it. That edge, and the node it reaches, join the tree.
Each step reduces the outside set by one node, so after n minus 1 additions every node is inside and the spanning tree is complete.
This inside versus outside split is the mental model to hold. Every decision Prim makes is about which outside node to bring in next.
The boundary between inside and outside is often called the cut, and Prim always acts on the cheapest edge crossing it.
The heart of Prim is the choice of which edge to add. Among all edges that lead from the current tree to a node not yet in it, Prim always takes the one with the smallest weight.

blocks.caption: Among all edges leaving the tree, Prim always adds the cheapest one
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761242-606928875.png

This is a greedy choice, and like Kruskal it is provably safe thanks to the cut property. The cheapest edge crossing the boundary between the tree and the rest is always part of some minimum spanning tree.

items: Look at every edge from an inside node to an outside node
These edges form the frontier of the growing tree
Always pick the cheapest frontier edge
Add both that edge and the new node it reaches

blocks.text: A subtle point: an outside node may be reachable by several frontier edges, but only the cheapest one matters for adding it.

Greedy but safe:

Taking the cheapest frontier edge never backfires. The cut property promises that edge belongs to some minimum spanning tree.
Ties between equally cheap frontier edges can be broken arbitrarily; every choice still leads to a valid minimum spanning tree.

content.title: 4. The Role of a Priority Queue

blocks.text: Scanning every frontier edge by hand at each step would be slow. Prim uses a priority queue, a min heap, to always have the cheapest candidate edge ready.

blocks.caption: A min heap holds candidate edges so the cheapest is always available
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761242-764761811.png
blocks.alt: The Role of a Priority Queue

blocks.text: Whenever a node joins the tree, Prim pushes all of its outgoing edges into the heap. To pick the next edge, it simply pops the smallest, ignoring any that lead to a node already in the tree.

Lazy deletion:

It is easiest to leave stale edges in the heap and skip them when popped if their target is already in the tree. This avoids fiddly deletions and keeps the code simple.
Without the heap, each step would rescan every frontier edge, which is wasteful. The heap turns that repeated search into a single logarithmic pop.
You can also store, per outside node, the cheapest edge seen so far and decrease its key, but the lazy skip approach is simpler and just as fast in practice.

content.title: 5. The Prim Algorithm Step by Step

blocks.text: The procedure is short once the pieces are in place.

blocks.caption: Start at one node and repeatedly pull in the nearest node via the cheapest edge
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761242-902909607.png
blocks.alt: The Prim Algorithm Step by Step

items: Start at any node and mark it as in the tree
Push all its edges into a min heap
Pop the cheapest edge; if it reaches a new node, add that node and edge
Push the new node edges into the heap
Repeat until all nodes are in the tree

blocks.text: Trace it on a small graph: start at A, take the cheapest leaving edge to B, then the cheapest now leading to C, then to D. Four nodes joined with three edges gives the minimum spanning tree.
The very first pop uses a weight of zero for the start node, which simply seeds the tree without adding any real edge weight.
From then on, every accepted pop contributes exactly one real edge and one new node to the tree.
The stopping condition is simply that all n nodes have joined, which happens after n minus 1 real edges are added.
The implementation is a min heap of weight and node pairs, plus a boolean array marking which nodes are already in the tree.
Each edge is pushed at most once and popped at most once, and the boolean check discards any stale entry cheaply.
The boolean array is what makes lazy deletion work: stale heap entries pointing at already added nodes are discarded the moment they surface.
Notice the total accumulates the popped weight, so the seed weight of zero contributes nothing and the answer is the true tree cost.
Prim optimality rests on the same cut property that justifies Kruskal. Consider the cut that separates the nodes already in the tree from those outside.

The cut property guarantees that the cheapest edge crossing any cut belongs to some minimum spanning tree. Prim always adds exactly that edge for the cut between inside and outside, so every edge it picks is provably safe.

items: The tree so far and the rest form a cut
Prim adds the cheapest edge crossing that cut
The cut property says that edge is safe for an MST
So the final tree is guaranteed to be minimum

blocks.text: The same exchange argument as Kruskal applies: swapping in the cheapest crossing edge and removing a costlier one never raises the total weight.
Since the swap is never harmful, an optimal tree containing Prim chosen edge always exists, which is exactly what safety means.
With a binary heap, Prim runs in the same league as Kruskal.

items: Time: O(E log V) using a binary heap
Each edge is pushed and popped at most once, each heap operation is O(log V)
Space: O(V plus E) for the heap and the adjacency lists
With a Fibonacci heap it improves in theory, but a binary heap is standard in practice

blocks.text: This matches Kruskal asymptotically, so the choice between them comes down to the shape of the graph rather than raw speed.
In big O terms Prim and Kruskal are the same, so neither dominates the other on running time alone.
The practical difference comes from constants and from which graph representation you already have on hand.
Both algorithms produce a minimum spanning tree, but they grow it differently and suit different inputs.

items: Kruskal sorts all edges and merges components with union find
Prim grows one tree from a start node using a priority queue
Kruskal is natural for sparse graphs given as an edge list
Prim is natural for dense graphs given as adjacency lists

blocks.text: If the graph is dense and you already have adjacency lists, Prim avoids sorting every edge and is often the more convenient choice.

items: Kruskal: edge list, global sort, union find, great for sparse graphs
Prim: adjacency lists, growing tree, heap, great for dense graphs
Both are greedy and both are provably optimal
Pick by graph density and representation, not correctness

content.title: 10. Dense Graphs and the Array Variant

blocks.text: For very dense graphs, where the number of edges approaches the square of the number of nodes, there is a simpler variant of Prim that skips the heap entirely.

Instead of a priority queue, it keeps an array of the cheapest known edge to each outside node, and each step scans that array to find the minimum. This is O(V squared), which can actually beat the heap version when the graph is dense.

Match the tool to the density:

Use the heap based Prim for sparse graphs and the simple array based Prim for very dense ones. The array version trades a log factor per edge for a linear scan per node.
On a dense graph the number of edges is close to V squared, so an O(V squared) scan can be cheaper than doing E log V heap operations.
This array variant is also delightfully simple to code, with no heap at all, just a linear search for the nearest outside node each round.
Prim solves the same real problems as any minimum spanning tree algorithm.

items: Designing least cost networks of cable, road, or pipe
Building a cheap backbone to connect facilities
Clustering by growing connections between nearby points
Any setting where a dense graph must be connected at minimum cost

blocks.text: When the graph is dense and stored as adjacency lists, Prim is frequently the go to method for these tasks.
Anywhere Kruskal applies, Prim applies too, since they solve the identical problem. The choice is about efficiency on the given graph.
For dense, adjacency listed graphs, Prim often needs less setup because it skips sorting the entire edge set.

content.title: 12. Pitfalls and How to Approach It

blocks.text: Keep these points in mind to use Prim correctly.

items: Skip heap entries whose target is already in the tree, or you will double count
Start from any node; the resulting total weight is the same regardless
On a disconnected graph, Prim only spans the component of its start node
Use a 64 bit total if edge weights are large, to avoid overflow

blocks.text:
Choosing between Prim and Kruskal:

Ask about the graph. Sparse and edge listed favours Kruskal; dense and adjacency listed favours Prim. Both are correct, so decide by efficiency and convenience.
One more caution: remember to seed the heap before the loop, or it starts empty and the tree never grows.
And as always, confirm the graph is connected, since Prim from one node cannot reach a separate component.
Prim is the greedy, node driven way to build a minimum spanning tree.

items: It grows one tree outward from a start node
At each step it adds the cheapest edge to a node not yet included
A min heap keeps the cheapest frontier edge ready
It runs in O(E log V), the same league as Kruskal
The cut property makes its greedy choice provably optimal

blocks.text: When you need the cheapest connecting tree of a dense graph, grow it with Prim: start anywhere, and keep pulling in the nearest node until the whole graph is joined.
Picture a flood spreading from a source, always flowing along the cheapest available channel to reach the next dry node.
